content: 1. Viral load monitoring is being conducted to assess the effectiveness of antiretroviral therapy (ART). If viral load tests are only performed on patients who have failed ART, the data may be skewed towards higher viral load counts, underestimating the rate of viral suppression. 2. In settings where routine viral load monitoring is not available, population-based or drug-resistance surveys may substitute for data from HIV patient monitoring systems. 3. Viral suppression is a critical goal of HIV treatment and represents the third 90 in the UNAIDS 90-90-90 targets. Patients on ART who achieve and maintain viral suppression significantly reduce their risk of disease progression and HIV transmission. 4. The denominator for viral load suppression indicators includes all patients with at least one recorded viral load test during the reporting period. Patients who transferred out of the facility before the end of the reporting period are excluded. 5. The numerator includes patients from the denominator whose viral load during the reporting period was recorded as less than 1,000 copies/mL. Patients who transferred out are also excluded. 6. At the national level, patients transferring into a facility (TI) should equal those transferring out (TO), and these do not need to be separately accounted for. 7. Disaggregation of data is performed by sex and age groups. For paper-based systems, age groups are categorized as <15 and 15+. For electronic systems, more detailed age groups are used, such as <1, 1–4, 5–9, 10–14, 15–19, and 20+. 8. Key viral load suppression indicators provide a comprehensive overview of viral suppression rates among the patient population. These indicators measure the proportion of patients who have received a viral load test result and achieved suppression after a fixed duration on ART. 9. The number of new ART patients provides facilities and programs with an understanding of the scale of implementing the treat all approach. This data helps in planning for adherence preparation, baseline monitoring, and lifelong ART provision. 10. Initially, the number of new ART patients may increase substantially but should stabilize and eventually decrease as new HIV infections decline, reducing the number of individuals requiring treatment. 11. ART retention indicators measure the percentage of patients who remain alive and on ART after 12 months. This data helps identify reasons for loss to follow-up (LTF), treatment cessation, or mortality. 12. For pregnant women, the percentage of those with known HIV status is calculated by counting those tested for HIV during antenatal care (ANC) or those already aware of their HIV-positive status. This data is reconciled with delivery records to avoid double counting. 13. The percentage of HIV-positive pregnant women who received ART during pregnancy is calculated by identifying those who delivered within the past 12 months and started ART before their expected delivery date (EDD). This data is reconciled with ANC and labor and delivery (L&D) registers. 14. For HIV-exposed infants, indicators measure the percentage who started cotrimoxazole (CTX) prophylaxis within two months of birth. These indicators are derived from the HIV-exposed infant (HEI) register and assess essential aspects of HEI care, including maternal ART receipt. 15. ART coverage during tuberculosis (TB) treatment is a critical indicator, as both treatments are necessary to reduce mortality in HIV-positive TB patients. This data is reconciled between TB monitoring systems and ART registers. 16. The number of patients starting TB preventive therapy is recorded and reconciled with TB registers to ensure accurate reporting and linkage to ART initiation. 17. Disaggregation of data for TB/HIV indicators is performed by sex and age (<15 and 15+). This ensures a detailed understanding of treatment coverage and outcomes across different demographic groups. 18. The revised definition of newly enrolled in HIV care to started on ART aligns with the treat all guidelines, emphasizing prompt ART initiation for all people living with HIV (PLHIV), including those with active TB. 19. Facilities must reconcile ART registers with other registers, such as maternal and child health (MCH) or TB registers, to ensure accurate data collection and avoid duplication. Unique identifiers and ART start dates are used as reference points. 20. For pregnant women, ART initiation is categorized as either prior to pregnancy or during pregnancy, based on the ART start date relative to the estimated or actual date of delivery. This helps assess the timing and coverage of ART during pregnancy.
